note: Silent-success detector families for scripts/silent-success-scan.sh.
A 'silent success' is code that REPORTS a successful production operation
without doing the work: a stub that returns OK, a handler that swallows an
error and returns nil, a function whose body is a TODO. These pass every
type check and every test that only asserts 'no error', which is exactly why
they reach production.
EVERY family below ships enabled:false, so a fresh DevGate install is GREEN.
These are illustrative starting points, not prescriptions — the patterns that
matter are the ones specific to YOUR codebase. Enable a family only after you
have allowlisted the existing occurrences you intend to keep (see
.guardrails/silent-success-allowlist.json), otherwise the gate goes red on
your first run.
Entry shape:
family    — stable id, reported on every hit
language  — informational grouping
regex     — Python re syntax, matched per line
file_glob — repo-relative globs OR bare basenames; a hit outside them is
ignored. Keep families narrow: a broad regex over a whole tree
produces noise that trains people to ignore the gate.
enabled   — false by default; opt in deliberately
note      — why this pattern is suspicious

rules.note: Announces a finished production operation. Verify the work is real and not a placeholder log line.
Rust stub reporting success with no effect. Legitimate in many places — scope this to the specific stub-prone modules before enabling.
A todo!/unimplemented! on a shipped code path panics in production instead of doing the work.
Error assigned to _ and then success returned: the failure is discarded and the caller is told everything worked.
A literal success envelope. Confirm it reflects a real result rather than a stubbed handler.
A function body that is a TODO returns None and reads as success to every caller.
Signal handler declared with no body. The UI reacts as if wired up while nothing happens. (Check the following line is not the real body.)
